analysis.one_liner: Cuts acid rain pollution in half and forces cleaner cars, fuels, and factory emissions nationwide.
analysis.headline: The Clean Air Act Amendments of 1990 became law: the Senate passed it 89-11, the House approved the final version 401-25, and President George H.W. Bush signed it on November 15, 1990 as Public Law 101-549.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill rewrote the nation's air pollution law. It forces power plants to cut sulfur dioxide by 10 million tons and nitrogen oxides by about 2 million tons from 1980 levels to fix acid rain, sets much stricter tailpipe and fuel standards for cars, and for the first time sets national limits on the toxic chemicals factories release into the air. It creates a tradeable permit system so power plants can cut pollution the cheapest way, funds retraining for workers who lose their jobs because of the new rules, and bans leaded gasoline. Utilities, refiners, automakers, and chemical plants bear the compliance costs, much of which gets passed on to customers through electric and gasoline prices.
analysis.who_benefits: Everyone who breathes, especially people in cities with smog, neighborhoods near factories releasing toxic chemicals, and regions downwind of coal plants suffering acid rain. The law also gives up to 26 weeks of extra income support and job training to workers laid off because companies had to comply.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Urban residents, asthma sufferers, downwind communities

how_it_helps.text: Requires nationwide reductions of 10 million tons of sulfur dioxide and roughly 2 million tons of nitrogen oxides from 1980 levels to control acid rain.

Sets a national goal of reducing cancer incidence attributable to toxic air pollutants by 75 percent, and requires emission standards for every category of major source of hazardous air pollutants within ten years.
Phases in stricter emissions standards for cars and light trucks beginning with model year 1994 and requires onboard systems that capture at least 95 percent of refueling vapors.
Requires cleaner reformulated gasoline in the smoggiest cities, oxygenated gasoline in carbon monoxide areas, low-sulfur diesel, and bans leaded gasoline after December 31, 1995.
Requires operating permits for major pollution sources with public access to permit applications, compliance plans, and monitoring reports, funded by fees of at least $25 per ton.
Authorizes job training, adjustment assistance, and needs-related payments for workers adversely affected by compliance with the Clean Air Act.

analysis.who_pays: Electric utilities, oil refiners, automakers, and industrial plants pay for scrubbers, reformulated fuels, new vehicle technology, and monitoring. Utilities are barred from charging low-income ratepayers for compliance costs, but the rest of the expense is generally recovered through electric bills and gasoline prices.

drawbacks.text: Existing polluters received their sulfur dioxide allowances free of charge, handing incumbents valuable emission rights at no cost while new plants must buy allowances on the market.

Gasoline sold in carbon monoxide areas must contain at least 2.7 percent oxygen, and reformulated gasoline must meet minimum oxygen content — a requirement that guarantees demand for oxygenate additives regardless of whether they are the cheapest way to clean the air.

The bill includes carve-outs: small refineries get special diesel allowances, Alaska and Hawaii are exempt from some diesel sulfur limits, and oil and gas stripper wells are excluded from ozone nonattainment requirements.
Compliance costs for power plants and refineries are large and are recovered largely through higher electricity rates and fuel prices, so consumers share the bill.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The health and environmental gains — roughly half of acid-rain-causing power plant pollution gone, national toxic emission limits for the first time, and dramatically cleaner cars and fuels — are large and were achieved at lower cost than command-and-control rules would have imposed, thanks to permit trading. The honest complaints are that existing polluters got their emission rights free, the oxygenate mandate locked in an expensive fuel requirement, and consumers ultimately foot much of the compliance bill through utility and gasoline prices.

outcome.mechanism: Both chambers passed it by overwhelming bipartisan votes — 89-11 in the Senate and 401-25 in the House on the final package — and President Bush signed it on November 15, 1990 as Public Law 101-549.

narrative.text: Introduced by Senator Baucus on September 14, 1989 and referred to the Environment and Public Works Committee, which held three days of hearings in October 1989 and reported it favorably on December 20, 1989.
The Senate debated the bill for weeks from January through early April 1990 and passed it 89-11, with 50 of 55 Democrats and 39 of 45 Republicans in favor.

The House took up the Senate bill in May 1990, struck its text and inserted the provisions of its own similar bill H.R. 3030, and passed it without objection, then insisted on its amendments and requested a conference.
A large conference committee spanning six House committees met repeatedly from July through October 1990 and agreed to file the conference report on October 26, 1990.
The House adopted the conference report 401-25 (248 of 257 Democrats and 153 of 175 Republicans in favor) and the Senate followed the next day, 89-10.
President George H.W. Bush signed the measure on November 15, 1990; it became Public Law 101-549.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Ordinary people gained cleaner air and the first national toxic emission limits. Utilities and refiners also did better than feared: instead of rigid technology mandates they received free, tradeable emission allowances, credits for cleaner fuels, and guaranteed oxygenate demand.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The public, plus utilities trading allowances

sides.party_line_note: Both parties backed it heavily at every stage: the Senate passed it 89-11 with 50 of 55 Democrats and 39 of 45 Republicans in favor, and the House adopted the final package 401-25, with more than 9 in 10 members of each party voting yes.

industries.note: Power plants must cut sulfur dioxide 10 million tons and nitrogen oxides 2 million tons from 1980 levels, but they receive allowances free of charge and may trade, bank, and auction them, giving incumbents a valuable emission-rights market and flexibility instead of rigid rules. Compliance costs are recovered from customers, with low-income ratepayers shielded by rate rules.

The law mandates minimum oxygen content in gasoline sold in carbon monoxide areas (at least 2.7 percent) and in reformulated gasoline, guaranteeing demand for oxygenates, and gives ethanol blends a one-pound volatility waiver. It served air quality goals but locked in demand for the oxygenate industry regardless of cost.

Refiners must produce reformulated gasoline for smoggy cities, cut diesel sulfur to 0.05 percent, and stop selling leaded gasoline after 1995. In exchange they gain captive reformulated-gasoline markets in nonattainment cities, tradable credits for exceeding oxygen and benzene specs, and special allowances for small refineries.

Stricter tailpipe standards phase in from model year 1994, onboard refueling vapor recovery and onboard diagnostics are required, and clean-fuel fleets are mandated in the worst smog areas. Costs land on new-car buyers and fleet operators.

industries.industry: Chemical and industrial plants emitting hazardous air pollutants
industries.note: For the first time, federal emission standards apply to all major sources of listed toxic air pollutants, with fines up to $1,000,000 per day for knowing releases that endanger people, plus accidental-release prevention planning and a new Chemical Safety and Hazard Investigation Board.

Incinerators must meet performance standards for dioxins, mercury, lead, and acid gases, monitor emissions continuously, train and certify operators, and manage ash under landfill liner rules — costs borne by the facilities and the communities they serve.

industries.industry: Small oil and gas stripper-well operators
industries.note: Title VIII exempts low-output oil and gas wells from most ozone nonattainment requirements, sparing a politically connected segment of the industry the compliance costs its larger competitors face.
